source.title: Towards Knowledge Exchange: State-of-the-Art and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: In knowledge-base mapping generation, how can mapping rules be generated for metadata-data correspondences, where a source data value must become target metadata such as a property name, or target data must become metadata, rather than simply mapping source concepts, properties, or paths to target concepts, properties, or paths?

evidence.quote: One important type of correspondence that, to the best of our knowledge, is not considered in KMGTs is metadata-data (MAD) correspondences [40,51]. Such correspondences articulate the need for a mapping that transforms data values to metadata (e.g., a property name) or vice versa. Arguably, such transformations may be more prevalent in KBs than in relational or semi-structured models. Generating proper mappings from MAD correspondences can be challenging.

accepted.question_text: For knowledge-base mapping generation tools, how can complex correspondences be handled when the correspondence says that a function transforms one or more source values into target values, a filter must be imposed on transferred source values, constraints should be added for invented target values, or source values must be aggregated even though knowledge bases use an open-world data model?

evidence.quote: Another type of important correspondence which needs further investigation is complex correspondences which indicate that a function can be used to transform a (set of) source value(s) into a (set of) target value(s), or that a filter should be imposed on source values that are being transferred.

One other interesting example of such correspondences are those that require aggregation over values in the source. Note that aggregating values is not a trivial task specially in KBs since KBs adhere to an open-world data model [18].

accepted.question_text: How can data-driven or example-based mapping generation approaches be adapted to knowledge-base mapping generation tools, especially when many knowledge bases are web-scale and therefore natural candidates for using data examples rather than only schema-level correspondences?

evidence.quote: In the future, it is important to understand how data driven approaches can be adopted in KMGTs particularly due to the web scale nature of many KBs making them ideal settings for using data examples.

accepted.question_text: Can knowledge-base mapping generation tools generate useful mappings from mixed evidence that may be incomplete or incorrect, including source-to-target correspondences, source constraints, mined join paths, data examples, and automatically generated examples from the Linked Open Data cloud?

evidence.quote: An important research direction for KGMTs is mapping generation that can use incomplete or incorrect correspondences and data examples, perhaps leveraging automatically generated examples from the Linked Open Data (LOD) cloud.

accepted.question_text: Can a knowledge-base mapping generation tool collectively learn correspondences, data examples, and mapping rules by combining logical and statistical reasoning, while still handling deep structural and semantic heterogeneity between two knowledge bases that cannot be resolved by simple same-as, isa, or equivalent-class axioms?

evidence.quote: In the spirit of fully combining logical and statistical reasoning, a KGMT that collectively learns correspondences, examples, and mappings would be an important milestone.

Some work including ILIADS [72], PARIS [71], and CODI [41] do this for ontology merging (learning same-as, isa, and equivalent-class axioms to merge two ontologies within a domain), but do not handle deep structural and semantic heterogeneity that cannot be resolved with simple axioms.

accepted.question_text: In user-in-the-loop refinement of knowledge-base mapping rules, how can a system choose examples that sufficiently illustrate the candidate rules, present those examples to domain experts, and incorporate domain-expert feedback that may be contradictory or wrong so that the final mapping rules can exchange data between two knowledge bases?

evidence.quote: We are currently working on approaches for interacting with domain experts, by finding examples which are sufficient illustrations [77] of rules generated by Kensho and incorporating the feedback to improve and refine the final set of mapping rules which can be used to exchange data between two KBs.

accepted.question_text: Can knowledge-base profiling and mining improve mapping quality by using available or automatically inferred constraints, such as cardinality constraints, functional-property constraints, inverse-functional-property constraints, disjointness constraints, join paths, or other mined dependencies, to resolve ambiguous property-path choices in source-to-target mappings?

evidence.quote: In general, we feel that KB profiling and mining may be helpful in improving mapping quality, in a similar way that database profiling and dependency mining [1] has been used to mine for join paths or other constraints that can guide mapping generation.

accepted.question_text: If positive or negative examples are available for a knowledge-base mapping task, can rule-mining methods identify important paths or rules and enrich the source or target ontologies with induced constraints in a way that helps generate better mapping rules?

evidence.quote: It is interesting to see whether enriching the source/target ontologies with additional induced constraints produced by running a rule mining algorithm can help generate better mapping rules.

accepted.question_text: How can formal theory for knowledge-base exchange, including universal solutions, universal UCQ-solutions, and UCQ-representations for DL-LiteR knowledge bases, guide knowledge-base mapping generation tools that consider target constraints, and can that theory be used to create tools whose generated mappings have specified formal properties?

evidence.quote: An important research question is how to use this formal work to guide KMGTs and if we can use the theory to create tools that produce mappings with certain formal properties.

accepted.question_text: How can knowledge exchange add and merge source data into a target knowledge base that is already populated, when inference in knowledge bases is complex and practical solutions also need deduplication, record linkage, same-as links, and conflict resolution for values?

evidence.quote: An interesting open problem is to understand how to do this in KBs where inference is more complex. In addition, practical solutions will need to use deduplication and record linkage to create links such as same-as and resolve conflicts in values.

accepted.question_text: How can knowledge-base mapping generation tools scale to large source and target knowledge bases by using methods more sophisticated than simple slicing, such as modularization or partitioning, while still generating mapping rules efficiently?

evidence.quote: One of the most important challenges that KMGTs face is the scale of the KBs. Kensho uses a simple method for slicing the KBs in order to be able to deal with larger scale source and target [34]. However, more sophisticated methods such as modularization [36,45,70] or partitioning [38,67,69] can be adopted to help in efficient generation of mapping rules when dealing with large scale KBs.

accepted.question_text: Can declarative mapping languages for large knowledge bases, such as R2R, be used to express knowledge-base mapping rules in a form that can be optimized and then compiled into SPARQL or another execution language?

evidence.quote: An interesting open question is to study the use of declarative languages like R2R that can perhaps be optimized and then “compiled” into SPARQL or other execution languages.

accepted.question_text: How can execution of transformation queries produced by knowledge-base mapping generation tools be optimized when the generated SPARQL queries contain many nested OPTIONAL clauses, which are required for open-world knowledge-base integration tasks but are expensive because query engines often process them as left outer joins?

evidence.quote: We believe our approach (as well as many other KB integration approaches) can immensely benefit from research on how to optimize the execution of queries that use SPARQL OPTIONAL clauses.

accepted.question_text: What knowledge-base mapping generation methods are needed for ontology-based data access, where heterogeneous relational sources are accessed through a target knowledge base as a virtual view, mapping rules must support efficient query rewriting, and the source and target models have different expressive power?

evidence.quote: Additional research is needed on KGMTs to support the unique requirements of OBDA [46].

accepted.question_text: Can the knowledge-base exchange community build an iBench-like metadata or exchange-scenario generator for evaluating knowledge-base mapping generation tools, with parameters that control factors such as value invention, incomplete source and target knowledge bases, incomplete correspondences, cycles, and multiple alternative interpretations of a correspondence?

evidence.quote: However, these parameters are not as extensive as the iBench parameters and do not control important factors such as the use of value invention and the number of alternative interpretations for a correspondence.

To begin to address this, we recently proposed a new set of scenarios for KB exchange that covers settings that require value invention, incomplete source and target KBs, incomplete correspondences, and KBs containing cycles [33], though notably our work does not go as far as providing the KB equivalent of an iBench metadata (exchange scenario) generator.

accepted.question_text: How can researchers create shared open-source real-world scenarios and corpora for knowledge translation and exchange so that knowledge-base mapping generation tools can be evaluated comparably, including evaluation of ranking measures when several mappings are structurally consistent but differ in intended semantics?

evidence.quote: Currently there are not enough open source real world scenarios that can be used for settings which involve KBs.
We believe knowledge translation and exchange research can greatly benefit from a community effort which identifies corpora that can be shared to produce comparable evaluations of KGMT.

accepted.question_text: How can mapping repair and adaptation for knowledge translation be performed when source or target knowledge bases change over time, so that mappings remain valid or consistent without regenerating them from scratch and while preserving as much of the original mapping semantics and query-answering capability as possible?

evidence.quote: Unfortunately, to the best of our knowledge, there is not yet any work in this area for settings which involve source and target KBs.
It is important to see how various repair notions proposed in the literature can be used in the context of knowledge translation and to facilitate the mapping adaptation.

Document map: section 1 Introduction defines knowledge exchange and mapping rules; section 2 reviews current KB exchange and Kensho; section 3 Challenges and Opportunities contains likely open-question regions in subsections 3.1 Mapping Generation: Input Evidence, 3.2 Mapping Refinement, 3.3 Knowledge Exchange, 3.4 Scalability and Optimization, 3.5 Application to other Integration Problems, 3.6 Evaluation, and 3.7 Evolution. Definitions indexed included KB, mapping rules/schema mappings, correspondences, KMGT/KGMT, Kensho, OBDA, universal solutions, R2R, SPARQL OPTIONAL, OAEI, and mapping repair.
